questions.stem: After unifying China in 221 BCE, King Zheng of Qin took a new title, Qin Shi Huangdi, meaning:
options: ‘Son of Heaven of Zhou’
‘Great King of the Seven States’
‘Lord of the Yellow River’
‘First Emperor of Qin’
questions.explanation: Shi means ‘first’, and huangdi combined two words linked to legendary sage rulers, creating a title above that of king. He intended his descendants to rule as Second, Third and later emperors for ever.

questions.stem: The Qin divided the empire into commanderies and counties governed by appointed officials. This replaced:
options: the Han practice of letting each province choose its own emperor
a system in which Buddhist monasteries collected taxes for the state
the Zhou practice of granting hereditary territories to nobles and relatives
a system of elected governors chosen by the people of each of the local districts
questions.explanation: The junxian system put salaried officials, who could be moved or dismissed, in charge of local government, ending the hereditary fiefs of the Zhou fengjian system. The Han came after the Qin, and Buddhism arrived later still.

questions.stem: Which set of Qin reforms was designed to unify the empire economically and culturally?
options: Elected local councils, free trade and an open border along the north
The examination system, a Confucian academy and a salt monopoly
Standard script, weights and measures, coinage and cart axle widths
A single religion, a ban on farming and an end to all taxation
questions.explanation: The Qin standardised writing, units of measurement, currency and even axle lengths so carts fitted the same road ruts. The Confucian academy and salt monopoly were Han measures under Emperor Wu.

questions.stem: Why was standardising the written script among the most lasting of the Qin reforms?
options: It was abandoned by the Han, so the Qin script survived only on the Terracotta Army
It let officials across regions with different spoken languages read the same documents
It forced every person in the empire to speak the dialect of the Qin capital at home
It replaced Chinese characters with an alphabet that was easier for peasants to learn
questions.explanation: A single script allowed laws and orders to be read throughout the empire, whatever local speech was used, and helped create a shared written culture that outlasted the Qin. The Han kept and developed it; it was never an alphabet.

questions.stem: The Qin round bronze coin with a square hole in the centre was significant because it:
options: was the first coin in the world to be made of pure gold rather than bronze
was used only in trade with Rome along the newly opened Silk Road
carried a portrait of the First Emperor to show his divine status
replaced the many regional currencies with one coin for the whole empire
questions.explanation: The banliang coin replaced spade, knife and other regional money, helping trade and tax collection. Its shape was used in China for about two thousand years. It carried an inscription, not a portrait, and was made of bronze.

questions.stem: Under the Qin, the general Meng Tian is best known for:
options: writing the Records of the Grand Historian at the Han imperial court
designing the Dujiangyan irrigation system on the Min River in Sichuan
leading the first peasant rebellion that brought the Qin dynasty down
campaigning against the Xiongnu and building northern walls and roads
questions.explanation: Meng Tian drove the Xiongnu back from the Ordos region, linked earlier walls into a northern defensive line and built the Direct Road. The Shiji was written by Sima Qian, and Dujiangyan was built by Li Bing.

questions.stem: Lu Buwei held high office in Qin before King Zheng ruled in his own right. His role was as:
options: chancellor and regent for the young king, and patron of a major book
commander of the army that defeated Zhao at the Battle of Changping
the minister who advised the First Emperor to burn the books in 213 BCE
the eunuch who forged the First Emperor's will after his death in 210 BCE
questions.explanation: Lu Buwei, a wealthy merchant, became chancellor and dominated the court while Zheng was young, sponsoring the compilation known as the Lüshi Chunqiu. Zheng dismissed him in 237 BCE. Li Si advised the burning of books, and Zhao Gao forged the will.

questions.stem: Li Si, chancellor under Qin Shi Huangdi, is associated with:
options: the Daoist search for immortality and voyages to the eastern islands
the peasant uprising at Dazexiang and the founding of the Han dynasty
Legalist policies such as standardising script and the burning of books
the Confucian revival at court and the founding of the Imperial Academy
questions.explanation: Li Si, a pupil of Xunzi, shaped Qin Legalist policy, including the standard script and the proposal of 213 BCE to burn books that could be used to criticise the present by praising the past. The Imperial Academy belongs to the Han.

questions.stem: According to the Shiji, the Qin ordered in 213 BCE that books of history, poetry and philosophy be burned, but books on medicine, divination and farming be kept. What does this suggest about Qin aims?
options: The state wanted to stop scholars using the past to criticise the present, not end learning
The state wanted to destroy every form of writing so that no laws could be recorded at all in Qin
The state wanted to promote Confucian learning by removing the books of its rivals
The state wanted to collect every book in one library to share it with the Xiongnu
questions.explanation: Keeping practical works while destroying histories and classics in private hands shows the aim was control of political ideas. The Qin relied heavily on written law and administration, and it was hostile to Confucian scholars who cited ancient models.

questions.stem: Sima Qian, writing about a century later under the Han, reports that the First Emperor had hundreds of scholars buried alive. Why should a historian treat this account cautiously?
options: Sima Qian lived during the Qin and was himself one of the few scholars who survived it
The account is found only on the walls of the First Emperor's tomb near Xi'an
The Qin had no scholars, because no one in the Qin could read or write
Han writers had reason to portray the Qin as tyrants to justify the Han's own rise
questions.explanation: The Han presented themselves as rescuers from Qin cruelty, and stories of Qin tyranny served that purpose. Some historians doubt the details of the burial of scholars, though the Qin's hostility to critics is not in doubt. Sima Qian was born decades after the Qin fell.

questions.stem: Legalism provided the main ideas behind Qin government. Which Qin practice best reflects Legalist thinking?
options: Strict, publicly known laws with harsh punishments applied to all
Government by the moral example of a virtuous and caring ruler
Leaving people alone to follow the natural way without laws
Choosing officials through examinations in the Confucian classics
questions.explanation: Legalists such as Han Feizi held that order came from clear laws, rewards and punishments enforced impartially. Moral example is Confucian, minimal government Daoist, and examinations in the classics belong to the Han and later dynasties.

questions.stem: The Terracotta Army near Xi'an was discovered in 1974 by:
options: miners searching for gold
farmers digging a well
soldiers building a road
monks repairing a temple
questions.explanation: Local farmers digging a well struck fragments of terracotta figures, leading to excavations that revealed thousands of life-sized soldiers in pits near the First Emperor's tomb mound.

questions.stem: Which feature of the terracotta warriors has most impressed archaeologists?
options: Their faces, hairstyles and uniforms vary, and they were originally painted
They are all identical copies made from a single mould of the emperor's face
They are made of solid bronze, each one cast in a single piece
They are arranged facing the emperor's tomb, as though worshipping him
questions.explanation: Figures were made from standard body parts but finished individually, with varied faces, hair and armour, and were brightly painted. They are fired clay, not bronze, and mostly face east, away from the tomb, as if guarding it.

questions.stem: Pit 1 holds rows of infantry, Pit 2 a mix of cavalry, chariots and archers, and Pit 3 a small group of officers. Archaeologists usually interpret Pit 3 as:
options: a command post directing the army
a stable for the emperor's horses
a storeroom for unused clay figures
a tomb for the emperor's family
questions.explanation: Pit 3's arrangement of officers and a chariot suggests a headquarters. Together the three pits form an army arranged for battle, guarding the emperor in the afterlife.

questions.stem: The Shiji says the First Emperor's tomb contained rivers of mercury and a ceiling showing the heavens. Soil tests over the unexcavated mound found unusually high levels of mercury. What can a historian best conclude?
options: The tomb has now been fully excavated, and every detail in the Shiji has been confirmed by it
The mercury proves the tomb was robbed and destroyed soon after the emperor died
Sima Qian's account must be invented, because no tomb could contain mercury
The scientific evidence supports part of Sima Qian's account, though the tomb is unopened
questions.explanation: High mercury readings are consistent with the Shiji's description, but without excavation the details cannot be confirmed. The main tomb chamber has not been opened, partly to protect what may be inside.

questions.stem: The scale of the First Emperor's mausoleum best shows:
options: his wish to be buried humbly, like an ordinary farmer
the influence of Buddhist ideas about rebirth in China
the end of all belief in the afterlife under Legalism
his belief that his power would continue in the afterlife
questions.explanation: An underground army, officials, entertainers and treasures reflect a belief that the emperor would rule in the afterlife and needed protection. It also displayed his ability to command vast resources and labour. Buddhism reached China later.

questions.stem: The First Emperor died in 210 BCE while:
options: touring the eastern part of his empire
leading his army against the Xiongnu
fighting rebels at the gates of Xianyang
praying at the tomb of his Zhou ancestors
questions.explanation: He died on one of his tours of inspection. His chief officials hid the death for a time while they arranged the succession.

questions.stem: After the First Emperor's death, the eunuch Zhao Gao and the chancellor Li Si:
options: forged an order forcing the heir Fusu to kill himself and put Huhai on the throne
announced the death at once and crowned the eldest son Fusu as emperor in the capital
handed power to Liu Bang so that the empire would pass peacefully to the Han
divided the empire between themselves and ruled as the Second and Third Emperors
questions.explanation: The conspirators feared Fusu and the general Meng Tian, so they forged a decree ordering both to die and made the younger son Huhai the Second Emperor. Zhao Gao later had Li Si executed.

questions.stem: In 209 BCE the conscripts Chen Sheng and Wu Guang rebelled against the Qin. According to the Shiji, they did so because:
options: they had been chosen by the Mandate of Heaven at a ceremony at Mount Tai
the Xiongnu offered to pay them to open the gates of the Great Wall
heavy rain delayed them and lateness was punishable by death under Qin law
the Han emperor promised them land if they overthrew the Second Emperor
questions.explanation: Facing execution for arriving late, they reasoned that rebelling was no worse, and their revolt sparked uprisings across the empire. The story shows how harsh laws and heavy labour demands turned subjects against the Qin.

questions.stem: Which combination of factors best explains why the Qin collapsed so soon after the First Emperor's death?
options: A plague brought along the Silk Road that killed most of the Qin army
Harsh laws and labour demands, a disputed succession and widespread revolt
A Xiongnu invasion that captured the capital and killed the Second Emperor
A Confucian revolution led by scholars who had escaped the burning of books
questions.explanation: Heavy forced labour on walls, roads and the mausoleum, severe punishments, court intrigue under Zhao Gao and a weak Second Emperor combined to produce revolt across the former states. The Qin fell to Chinese rebels, not to the Xiongnu.

questions.stem: After the Qin collapsed, the two leading rebel commanders who fought for control of China were:
options: Wang Mang and Liu Xiu
Cao Cao and Dong Zhuo
Shang Yang and Li Si
Liu Bang and Xiang Yu
questions.explanation: Liu Bang, a commoner and minor official, and Xiang Yu, from a noble family of Chu, fought the Chu–Han war. Liu Bang won in 202 BCE and became Emperor Gaozu of the Han. Cao Cao and Dong Zhuo belong to the end of the Han.

questions.stem: The Western Han dynasty had its capital at:
options: Chang'an
Luoyang
Anyang
Nanjing
questions.explanation: The Western Han ruled from Chang'an, near modern Xi'an. The Eastern Han moved the capital to Luoyang. Anyang was the late Shang capital.

questions.stem: Emperor Gaozu kept much of the Qin system but also changed it. Which description of early Han government is most accurate?
options: He kept Qin-style commanderies but gave kingdoms to relatives, and eased taxes and laws
He abolished the commanderies and returned the whole empire to hereditary Zhou-style fiefs
He kept every Qin law unchanged and increased forced labour to rebuild the Great Wall
He made Confucianism the only state philosophy and founded the Imperial Academy
questions.explanation: Gaozu's mixed system combined Qin-style commanderies with semi-independent kingdoms, mostly for members of the Liu family, and he lightened Qin taxes and punishments. The Imperial Academy was founded later, under Emperor Wu.

questions.stem: After Gaozu's death, real power at court was held for about fifteen years by:
options: his widow, Empress Lü
the general Meng Tian
the historian Sima Qian
the Xiongnu ruler Modu
questions.explanation: Empress Lü dominated the court as empress dowager, placing members of her own clan in high positions. After her death in 180 BCE, officials and the Liu princes purged the Lü clan and enthroned Emperor Wen.

questions.stem: The reigns of Emperors Wen and Jing are remembered for:
options: the burning of books and the persecution of scholars
low taxes, frugal government and a recovering economy
huge new building projects such as the Grand Canal
the conquest of Rome and the opening of sea trade
questions.explanation: Wen and Jing reduced land taxes and punishments, avoided costly wars and let the economy recover. The Grand Canal was built centuries later under the Sui, and the burning of books was a Qin policy.

questions.stem: Empress Dowager Dou, mother of Emperor Jing, is known for favouring:
options: Huang-Lao Daoist ideas and resisting the rise of Confucians at court
Legalist policies and a return to the harsh punishments of the Qin
Buddhist teachings brought by monks along the Silk Road from India
an alliance with Wang Mang to take the throne from the Liu family
questions.explanation: Empress Dowager Dou supported Huang-Lao thought, which favoured light, non-interfering government, and she blocked Confucian officials early in Emperor Wu's reign. Confucianism advanced rapidly after her death. Wang Mang came over a century later.

questions.stem: In 154 BCE the Rebellion of the Seven States broke out under Emperor Jing. What caused it and what was its main consequence?
options: Confucian scholars revolted against the court; their defeat led to the burning of the books
Plans to cut the kings' lands provoked revolt; its defeat let the throne curb the kingdoms
Peasants rebelled against Qin laws; its success let them choose the first Han emperor
The Xiongnu invaded seven border states; their victory forced the Han to pay tribute
questions.explanation: Emperor Jing's adviser Chao Cuo proposed reducing the kingdoms, and the King of Wu led six other kings in revolt. The rebellion was crushed within months, and afterwards the kingdoms lost most of their power to the central government.

questions.stem: Under Emperor Wu (Wudi), the Han founded an Imperial Academy to train officials in:
options: Buddhist scripture
the Confucian classics
the Legalist law code
Daoist meditation
questions.explanation: Wudi established the Imperial Academy in 124 BCE, where students studied the Confucian classics to qualify for government office. This tied the bureaucracy to Confucian learning for centuries.

questions.stem: Historians sometimes describe Han government as ‘Confucian on the outside, Legalist on the inside’. What does this mean?
options: The Han banned Legalist books but secretly taught them in the Imperial Academy
Confucian ideals justified rule, while Qin-style laws and bureaucracy still did the governing
Confucian scholars ran the provinces, while Legalists controlled only the imperial palace itself
The Han followed Confucianism in peacetime and switched to Legalism only during wars
questions.explanation: The Han adopted Confucian moral language, ritual and education as the ideology of empire, but kept the centralised administration, laws and punishments inherited from the Qin. This blend shaped imperial Chinese government.

questions.stem: Emperor Wu introduced state monopolies on salt and iron. The main reason was to:
options: raise revenue to pay for his wars and expansion
lower the price of salt and iron for farmers
end the use of iron weapons in the empire
give merchants more control over these goods
questions.explanation: Wudi's long campaigns emptied the treasury, so the state took over the production and sale of salt and iron to raise money. The monopolies were later debated at court in 81 BCE, when Confucian critics argued they harmed the people.

questions.stem: Zhang Qian's missions to Central Asia for Emperor Wu were significant because they:
options: brought Buddhism to China and led to the building of temples in Chang'an
ended the war with the Xiongnu by arranging a marriage between the two royal courts
led to the conquest of India and the founding of a Han colony on its coast
gave the Han knowledge of western lands and led to the opening of Silk Road trade
questions.explanation: Zhang Qian was sent to seek allies against the Xiongnu and returned with detailed knowledge of Central Asian kingdoms, their horses and trade goods. This led to Han expansion westward and trade routes later called the Silk Road.

questions.stem: Which goods mainly travelled west from Han China along the Silk Road?
options: Glass and wool
Gold and ivory
Silk and lacquerware
Horses and grapes
questions.explanation: Chinese silk was the most prized export, along with lacquer goods. Horses, grapes and alfalfa came east into China from Central Asia, and glass came from the Mediterranean world.

questions.stem: Early in the Han dynasty, after a defeat in 200 BCE, the Han dealt with the Xiongnu through the heqin policy. This involved:
options: conquering the Xiongnu homeland and settling Chinese farmers
banning all trade with the Xiongnu and closing the frontier
sending princesses in marriage and gifts of silk and grain
building the Great Wall for the first time along the north
questions.explanation: Heqin, ‘peace through kinship’, bought peace with marriage alliances and regular gifts. Emperor Wu abandoned it in favour of war. Walls had already been built and linked under the Qin.

questions.stem: Emperor Wu's wars against the Xiongnu were debated at court. Which argument would a Confucian critic most likely have made?
options: The wars should be fought by Xiongnu soldiers hired to defend the Han frontier
The wars were justified because the Mandate of Heaven required constant expansion
The wars burdened the people and a virtuous ruler should win over others by example
The wars were too small and the empire should conquer every land beyond the frontier
questions.explanation: Confucian critics, as in the Debate on Salt and Iron, argued that costly wars and monopolies harmed ordinary people and that moral government, not force, should attract outsiders. Supporters of the wars stressed security and revenue.

questions.stem: Wang Mang interrupted Han rule by founding the Xin dynasty (9–23 CE). His reign ended after:
options: the Xiongnu captured Chang'an and placed him on the throne
he handed power back peacefully to the Liu family in 23 CE
the Yellow Turbans defeated his armies at the gates of Luoyang
radical reforms failed and floods and famine led to rebellion
questions.explanation: Wang Mang's land and currency reforms caused disruption, and a shift in the course of the Yellow River brought flooding and famine. Rebellions such as the Red Eyebrows followed, and he was killed in 23 CE. The Yellow Turbans rose much later, in 184 CE.

questions.stem: The Eastern (Later) Han dynasty moved the capital to:
options: Xianyang
Anyang
Luoyang
Chang'an
questions.explanation: Liu Xiu, Emperor Guangwu, restored the Han in 25 CE with Luoyang as the capital. Chang'an had been the Western Han capital, Xianyang the Qin capital.

questions.stem: In the late Eastern Han, why did palace eunuchs become so powerful?
options: They commanded the armies that had defeated the Xiongnu in the north
They were the only officials who had studied in the Imperial Academy
Young emperors relied on them against the powerful families of empresses
They were elected by the provinces to represent them at the imperial court
questions.explanation: Emperors who came to the throne as children were dominated by their mothers' families, and some used trusted eunuchs to break that control. Factional struggles between eunuchs, consort families and officials weakened the court.

questions.stem: The Yellow Turban Rebellion of 184 CE was led by Zhang Jue, who promised:
options: the conversion of the empire to Buddhism and the closing of Confucian schools
a new age of ‘Great Peace’ to replace a Han government that had lost Heaven's favour
a return to the Legalist laws of the Qin and the restoration of the Qin royal family
an alliance with the Xiongnu that would end the wars along the northern frontier
questions.explanation: Zhang Jue led a Daoist-inspired movement, the Way of Great Peace, drawing on peasants suffering from famine, epidemics and heavy taxes. Its claim that a new heaven would replace the old challenged the Han's Mandate.

questions.stem: Although the Yellow Turbans were defeated, the rebellion contributed to the fall of the Han. Which explanation is most accurate?
options: The Yellow Turbans invited the Xiongnu into China, who then destroyed the dynasty
The rebellion led the Han to abandon Luoyang and move the capital to Xianyang
Generals given troops to fight the rebels became warlords beyond the court's control
The rebels captured the emperor and forced him to give the throne to Zhang Jue himself
questions.explanation: To suppress the revolt, the court let regional commanders raise their own armies. These generals, such as Dong Zhuo, then fought over power, leaving the emperor a figurehead. The Han formally ended in 220 CE.

questions.stem: In 189 CE the warlord Dong Zhuo seized the capital. What did he do there?
options: Founded the Qin dynasty again and declared himself First Emperor
Signed a treaty with Rome to open sea trade from Luoyang
Deposed the emperor, installed a puppet and later burned Luoyang
Restored full power to the emperor and the eunuchs at court
questions.explanation: Dong Zhuo replaced the young emperor with Emperor Xian, moved the court to Chang'an and burned Luoyang. His brutal rule showed that the dynasty now depended on the generals. He was killed in 192 CE.

questions.stem: The Shiji (Records of the Grand Historian) was written by:
options: Ban Zhao
Sima Xiangru
Han Feizi
Sima Qian
questions.explanation: Sima Qian completed the Shiji during the reign of Emperor Wu, continuing work begun by his father, Sima Tan. It covers Chinese history from legendary times to his own day. Ban Zhao wrote Lessons for Women.

questions.stem: Sima Qian chose to suffer castration rather than death after defending a disgraced general, so that he could finish the Shiji. How might his experience affect a historian's use of the work?
options: It shows that Sima Qian supported every policy of Emperor Wu without any reservation
It proves that the Shiji was written by a committee of officials rather than by a single historian
His suffering under Emperor Wu may shape how critically he presents the emperor and his court
It means the Shiji was written before the Qin dynasty and is an eyewitness account of it
questions.explanation: Sima Qian's punishment by Emperor Wu gives him a personal perspective, and some readers detect criticism of Wu in his work. His careful use of sources makes the Shiji invaluable, but historians weigh his viewpoint like any other.

questions.stem: Ban Zhao's Lessons for Women advised women to be humble, obedient and hard-working. Which other view did she argue?
options: Women should be allowed to become emperor
Women should serve in the imperial army
Women should not marry or raise children
Girls as well as boys should be educated
questions.explanation: Ban Zhao accepted the Confucian hierarchy within the family, but argued that girls should be taught to read, so that they could serve their families properly. She was herself a scholar who helped complete the Book of Han.

questions.stem: Sima Xiangru's rhapsody on the imperial hunting park describes its vast size, rare animals and lavish hunts in rich detail. Historians use it mainly as evidence of:
options: the daily work of peasants farming the land around Chang'an
the methods used by the Han army against the Xiongnu
the spread of Buddhism among the scholars of the Han court
how court poetry glorified the emperor's wealth and power
questions.explanation: Sima Xiangru wrote fu (rhapsodies) for Emperor Wu's court. His description of the park celebrates imperial magnificence, so it shows how literature served the image of the emperor, though it exaggerates for effect.
